title: The Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP)
subtitle: How voice and video calls get encrypted and tamper-proofed without making the packets much bigger.
summary: SRTP is a profile of the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) that adds confidentiality, message authentication and replay protection to media streams, and the same for their control traffic, RTCP. It encrypts only the payload, leaves the RTP header readable, and appends a short authentication tag, so packets grow very little. All its session keys are derived from one master key supplied by a separate key management protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: SRTP adds security to the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP), which carries audio and video over the Internet. It encrypts the media, checks that packets were not altered, and blocks replayed packets, with very little extra data per packet. All of its keys are derived from one master key supplied by a separate key management protocol.

tldr.problem: RTP sends voice and video in the clear, so anyone on the path can listen, alter or replay it, and bulky security would hurt real-time and wireless use.
tldr.mechanism: SRTP encrypts the RTP payload with AES in counter mode, appends an HMAC-SHA1 tag over the header and payload, tracks a 48-bit packet index for replay checks, and derives all session keys from one master key.
tldr.outcome: It is the standard way to protect RTP media, used with key exchange protocols such as DTLS-SRTP and SDES, and it is the foundation of WebRTC media security.

today: SRTP is how real-time media is protected in most secure voice and video systems. WebRTC requires it, with keys set up by DTLS-SRTP (RFC 5764), and SIP-based telephony commonly uses it with keys carried in SDP (RFC 4568) or MIKEY. Newer ciphers such as AES-GCM (RFC 7714) are now widely preferred over the original AES-CM plus HMAC-SHA1 pair, but they still plug into the framework this RFC defines.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Real-time Transport Protocol, RTP (RFC 3550), carries audio and video over the Internet, and its companion RTCP carries the control feedback: who is in the session, how many packets arrived, when someone leaves. Neither one protects anything. Anyone who can see the packets can listen in, change them or replay them.

SRTP is defined as a profile of RTP, an extension of the audio/video profile in RFC 3551. Conceptually it is a "bump in the stack" between the RTP application and the transport layer: on the sending side it intercepts RTP packets and forwards equivalent SRTP packets, and on the receiving side it does the reverse. Secure RTCP (SRTCP) gives the control traffic the same treatment.

SRTP does not say how keys get to the two ends. That is left to a key management protocol (Section 8 gives guidance), which is why the same SRTP can be keyed in several different ways.
sections.plainLanguage: RTP carries audio and video, and its companion RTCP carries control feedback, but neither protects anything: anyone who sees the packets can listen, change them or replay them. SRTP sits between the application and the transport layer, turning RTP packets into protected ones. It does not say how keys reach the two ends.

sections.title: Goals and features
sections.content:
The security goals are confidentiality of RTP and RTCP payloads, and integrity of the entire RTP and RTCP packets together with protection against replay. These services are optional and independent of each other, with one exception: SRTCP integrity protection is mandatory, because tampering with RTCP could disrupt the whole stream.

The functional goals matter just as much. SRTP wants a framework that can be upgraded with new cryptographic transforms, a low bandwidth cost that preserves RTP header compression, low computational cost, a small code and memory footprint, limited packet expansion, and independence from the underlying network, with high tolerance of packet loss and re-ordering. That last point explains many design choices: every packet must be decryptable on its own.

One master key
A single master key yields all the session keys for SRTP and SRTCP through a key derivation function.
Key refresh
Session keys can be refreshed periodically, limiting how much ciphertext an attacker sees under one key.
Salting keys
Salts defend against pre-computation and time-memory tradeoff attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: SRTP aims to keep media payloads secret, to detect tampering with whole packets, and to stop replays. These services are optional, except that integrity protection for RTCP is mandatory. It also aims to add little size and processing cost, and to tolerate lost or reordered packets, so every packet must be decryptable on its own.

sections.title: The SRTP packet
sections.content:
An SRTP packet is an RTP packet with two changes. The RTP payload (including any RTP padding) is replaced by its encrypted form, the Encrypted Portion, which for the pre-defined ciphers is exactly the same size as the plaintext. And two fields are added at the end: an optional Master Key Identifier (MKI) of configurable length, and an authentication tag, which is RECOMMENDED and also of configurable length.

The RTP header itself is not encrypted. It travels in the clear so that header compression still works, which means payload type, timestamp and SSRC are visible to anyone watching. The Authenticated Portion is the RTP header followed by the Encrypted Portion; the MKI is not authenticated. When both services are used, encryption is applied before authentication on the sender, and the reverse on the receiver.

Only 8-bit alignment is assumed, so the MKI and tag can be any whole number of octets.
sections.plainLanguage: An SRTP packet is an RTP packet with an encrypted payload and up to two extra fields at the end: an optional Master Key Identifier (MKI) and an authentication tag. The RTP header stays readable so header compression still works. Authentication covers the header and the encrypted payload.

sections.title: Cryptographic contexts and the packet index
sections.content:
Each SRTP stream needs state at both ends, called the cryptographic context. It holds the master key and optional master salt, the cipher and authentication identifiers, an MKI setting, and counters of packets sent under each master key. A context is identified by the triplet of SSRC, destination network address and destination port. A packet with no matching context MUST be discarded.

RTP carries only a 16-bit sequence number, which wraps. SRTP therefore keeps a 32-bit rollover counter (ROC) and defines the packet index as i = 2^16 * ROC + SEQ, a 48-bit value that is never sent on the wire. The sender increments the ROC each time the sequence number wraps. The receiver keeps its own ROC and the highest sequence number seen, s_l, and estimates the index by picking the ROC candidate (ROC-1, ROC or ROC+1) that puts the index closest to its current position. This only fails if about 2^15 packets are lost or out of order.

The same key must never encrypt two packets with the same index and SSRC. The RFC caps a stream at 2^48 SRTP packets (and 2^31 SRTCP packets) per key, after which re-keying is required.
sections.plainLanguage: Each SRTP stream needs saved state at both ends, called the cryptographic context, which holds the keys and settings. RTP's 16-bit sequence number wraps around, so SRTP also keeps a rollover counter to form a longer packet index that is never sent. The same key must never encrypt two packets with the same index and SSRC.

sections.title: Packet processing and replay protection
sections.content:
The sender follows eight steps: find the context, determine the index, find the master key and salt, derive the session keys, encrypt the payload, append the MKI if used, compute and append the authentication tag, and update the ROC if needed. The receiver reverses this, but checks first and decrypts last. It looks up the context, estimates the index, finds the master key, derives session keys, checks the replay list, verifies the tag, then decrypts, then updates s_l, ROC and the replay list, and finally strips the MKI and tag.

Replay protection needs authentication, because without it the sequence number could be forged. The receiver keeps a replay list, normally a sliding window whose size, SRTP-WINDOW-SIZE, MUST be at least 64. A packet behind the window, or inside it but already seen, is rejected. A replayed packet or an "AUTHENTICATION FAILURE" means the packet MUST be discarded and the event SHOULD be logged.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender finds the context, derives the keys, encrypts the payload and adds an authentication tag. The receiver reverses this, but checks for replays and verifies the tag before it decrypts anything. Packets that are replayed or fail authentication must be discarded. Replay checking uses a sliding window of at least 64 packets.

sections.title: Secure RTCP
sections.content:
SRTCP follows SRTP but adds three mandatory fields to an RTCP compound packet: a 1-bit E flag, a 31-bit SRTCP index, and the authentication tag, plus the optional MKI. The E flag says whether this packet is encrypted. The index is carried explicitly, so the receiver does not need to estimate it. It starts at zero, increments by one modulo 2^31 for each packet, and is never reset on re-keying.

Encryption starts at the ninth octet, after the first header and sender SSRC. The first packet in the compound MUST be a sender or receiver report, and the random 32-bit encryption prefix from RTP MUST NOT be used. SRTCP authentication is mandatory because RTCP is the control channel; it has, for example, a BYE packet. The added fields are at least 14 octets for the pre-defined transforms, so the RTCP bandwidth calculation (avg_rtcp_size) must include them, or SRTCP would hog its share of the session bandwidth.
sections.plainLanguage: Secure RTCP (SRTCP) works like SRTP but adds a flag showing whether the packet is encrypted, an explicit 31-bit packet index and an authentication tag. Authentication is mandatory because RTCP controls the session. These extra fields add at least 14 octets, which the RTCP bandwidth calculation must count.

sections.title: Cryptographic transforms and key derivation
sections.content:
SRTP defines default algorithms so implementations interoperate. Encryption is AES in Segmented Integer Counter Mode (AES-CM): the keystream is AES applied to successive counter values, starting from IV = (k_s * 2^16) XOR (SSRC * 2^64) XOR (i * 2^16), and XORed onto the payload. AES in f8-mode is an optional alternative. There is also a mandatory NULL cipher. Integrity uses HMAC-SHA1 truncated to an 80-bit tag by default.

All session keys come from key derivation. A pseudo-random function (the default is AES-CM) is keyed with the master key and fed an input built from an 8-bit label, the master salt and the packet index divided by the key_derivation_rate. Labels 0x00 to 0x02 produce the SRTP encryption key, authentication key and salt; 0x03 to 0x05 do the same for SRTCP. With a rate of zero, derivation happens exactly once. Nonzero rates (powers of two up to 2^24) refresh the session keys periodically.

Defaults: 128-bit encryption key, 160-bit authentication key, 112-bit salts, 80-bit tag.

For SRTCP, the HMAC-SHA1 tag and key MUST NOT be shorter than these defaults.
sections.plainLanguage: By default SRTP encrypts with AES in counter mode and authenticates with HMAC-SHA1 truncated to an 80-bit tag. All session keys are derived from the master key and a salt using a pseudo-random function. A key derivation rate can refresh the session keys periodically.

sections.title: Key management and security considerations
sections.content:
The biggest danger is the "two-time pad": encrypting two different messages with the same keystream, which lets an attacker cancel it out. The IV includes both the packet index and the SSRC to prevent this, so SSRCs must be unique among streams that share a master key. The RFC REQUIRES automatic key management, since manual keying makes keystream reuse far more likely. A master key MUST NOT be shared among different RTP sessions.

Re-keying is done by tagging packets with an MKI or by using an optional <From, To> index range per master key. Weak or null authentication is allowed only under strict conditions: neither may be used if forwarding or access control decisions depend on the data, and null authentication MUST NOT be used if replay could matter or if forgery matters. An encrypted but unauthenticated stream can be altered bit by bit by an attacker who can guess the plaintext.

Header is visible
Payload type, SSRC and timestamp are not hidden. Use IPsec if you need that.
Length leaks
Stream-cipher encryption reveals the exact payload length.
Groups
A shared key proves only that some group member sent a packet, not which one.
sections.plainLanguage: The main danger is encrypting two different messages with the same keystream, which lets an attacker cancel the encryption out. The RFC therefore requires automatic key management and forbids sharing a master key between RTP sessions. The RTP header is not hidden, and encrypted data without authentication can be altered.

data.title: Packet index and AES-CM IV
data.code:
# 48-bit packet index (never sent on the wire)
i = 2^16 * ROC + SEQ

# Receiver estimate: choose v from { ROC-1, ROC, ROC+1 } (mod 2^32)
i = 2^16 * v + SEQ     # closest to 2^16 * ROC + s_l

# AES counter mode IV for each packet (128 bits)
IV = (k_s * 2^16) XOR (SSRC * 2^64) XOR (i * 2^16)

# Keystream: E(k_e, IV) || E(k_e, IV+1) || E(k_e, IV+2) ...
# Authentication: M = Authenticated Portion || ROC

items.title: Never reuse keystream
items.text: Index plus SSRC must be unique per key; automatic key management is REQUIRED.

items.title: Re-key before the limit
items.text: 2^48 SRTP packets or 2^31 SRTCP packets per key, whichever comes first.

items.title: Keep authentication on
items.text: Null or weak tags only for stateless, low-risk streams. SRTCP must always have strong ones.

items.title: Mind the group
items.text: Shared keys give integrity, not proof of which member sent a packet.
